title: To Erase, or Not to Erase: Robust Training-Free Concept Erasure with Preservation aware Adaptive Ranked Subspace Expansion

paper.title: To Erase, or Not to Erase: Robust Training-Free Concept Erasure with Preservation aware Adaptive Ranked Subspace Expansion
paper.abstract:
Abstract Concept erasure techniques (CETs) edit text-to-image diffusion models to erase undesired targets (e.g., NSFW content or copyrighted styles) while preserving model utility on image generation for benign concepts.
Current CETs often face a trade-off between erasure robustness and model utility: stronger edits erase target more reliably, but degrade model utility on non-target concepts and vice-versa.
A key source of this trade-off is how existing methods define what to erase and what to preserve.
Many CETs rely on static concept banks, where erase or retain concepts are manually specified, generated by Large Language Models (LLMs), or selected using CLIP-based image–text similarity.
However, such static banks do not explicitly model how prompts steer the diffusion model during denoising, leaving edited models vulnerable to triggers that can reintroduce the target while unintentionally suppressing nearby benign concepts.
We present Preservation aware Adaptive Ranked Subspace Expansion (PARSE) , a training-free framework for robust concept erasure in latent diffusion models.
Given a target, PARSE queries the diffusion model using classifier-free guidance to dynamically discover target-inducing erase concepts and nearby retain concepts from the model vocabulary. PARSE then edits the cross-attention value space with a preservation-aware projection that removes target directions while leaving retain directions intact.
To address triggers beyond the vocabulary-indexed search space, PARSE iteratively searches for re-emergence triggers using textual inversion and adaptively expands the erased subspace only when a new trigger direction does not conflict with retain semantics.
We further introduce Balanced Erasure Utility Score (BEUS) , a balanced erasure utility score that combines robustness (ASR under multiple attacks) and utility preservation (FID) via bounded monotone transforms and harmonic mean aggregation.
Extensive experiments across NSFW, artistic style, and object erasure, together with a large-scale robustness utility analysis over many CET baselines, show that PARSE achieves robust erasure across multiple concepts without sacrificing post-edit model utility. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image diffusion models are widely deployed for image generation from text prompts [ 31 , 39 ] , yet their ability to faithfully reproduce undesirable concepts (e.g., NSFW content or copyrighted styles) raises pressing safety and compliance concerns. Concept Erasure Techniques (CETs), a form of machine unlearning [ 22 , 16 , 58 , 8 , 53 ] address this by editing a pretrained model to suppress or erase user-specified targets while preserving model utility to generate benign non-target concepts. In practice, concept erasure demands a careful balance: robust erasure often degrades model utility [ 40 , 22 ] , whereas with inferior erasure [ 53 , 14 ] , the target can still re-emerge with semantically similar [ 40 , 54 ] , paraphrased [ 1 ] , or adversarial prompts [ 64 ] . First, many CETs 1 1 1 Detailed literature review and related works are provided in supplementary material. rely on static target concept sets [ 14 , 25 , 13 ] either pre-defined by humans, LLMs or retrieved using image-text similarity in proxy CLIP [ 37 ] embedding space. Since these sets are curated without explicitly modeling how prompts steer the denoising trajectory [ 33 , 39 , 63 ] in diffusion models, they fail to capture diffusion-grounded triggers [ 14 , 25 , 13 ] and leave the erased model vulnerable to re-emergence attacks [ 35 ] . Second, adversarially robust CETs [ 64 , 20 , 23 ] suppress often over-suppress and inadvertently erase semantically adjacent concepts (e.g., removing “garbage truck” also suppresses “tow truck”), compromising generation quality and diversity [ 1 , 55 ] . Finally, existing CETs typically report robustness and utility separately [ 15 , 59 , 52 ] , making it difficult to evaluate whether a CET truly achieves an effective erasure-utility balance. We introduce PARSE , a preservation-aware and trigger-adaptive concept erasure framework for latent diffusion models. Unlike existing methods that rely on predefined or proxy concept pools [ 6 , 26 , 29 ] , project target directions without a target-conditioned retain bank [ 59 ] , or finetune on discovered adversarial prompts without enforcing a retain-orthogonal residual expansion [ 52 , 15 , 23 ] , our method (i) dynamically discovers target-adjacent concepts by querying the diffusion model using classifier-free guidance [ 19 ] rather than proxy embeddings, (ii) replaces human/LLM-defined anchor sets with diffusion-vocabulary knowledge-bank retrieval (zero-shot), treating the target as a query to retrieve target-adjacent tokens that define erase/retain banks, (iii) performs preservation-aware value-subspace projection that explicitly protects retain semantics while removing target directions, and (iv) adaptively expands the erased subspace by iteratively discovering triggers that can reintroduce the target, while preserving model utility. Therefore, the key idea of PARSE is an end-to-end zero-shot method that defines what to erase, what to retain, and when to expand, using priors from the diffusion model. Together, these design principles yield robust concept erasure for latent diffusion models across diverse concept categories without sacrificing post-edit model utility. Our contributions are threefold: • We propose PARSE , a robust training-free concept erasure framework that unifies diffusion-grounded ranked subspace construction, preservation-aware projection, and trigger-guided adaptive subspace expansion. • We introduce BEUS , an erasure utility balance score that jointly measures erasure robustness (ASR) and model utility preservation (FID) via bounded monotone transforms and harmonic-mean aggregation. • We conduct extensive experiments across NSFW, artistic style, and object erasure under multiple attacks and datasets, including a large-scale robustness-utility balance analysis over many CET baselines with BEUS , showing that PARSE improves erasure robustness, preserving model utility.

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: The goal of concept erasure in latent diffusion models is to prohibit image generation of undesired target concept(s) specified by the user (e.g., nudity ) . In this section, we discuss how text-to-image latent diffusion models generate images from text prompts, and how value-space projection in diffusion cross-attention layers can be used for Concept Erasure.

sections.heading: 3 Preservation aware Adaptive Ranked Subspace Expansion ( PARSE ) for balanced Concept Erasure
sections.text: Given a latent diffusion model M 0 M_{0} and target concept(s), CET returns an edited model M target M_{\texttt{\normalsize target}} that suppresses target generation while preserving utility on non-target concepts. To balance erasure and utility, PARSE has three components: (i) Ranked Subspace ( Knowledge Search ), (ii) Preservation-aware Subspace Projection, and (iii) Adaptive Subspace Expansion. We describe each component below and how they compose into PARSE . Figure 2 : PARSE builds diffusion-grounded erase and retain banks via two-stage Knowledge Search, applies preservation-aware value-space projection to remove target directions while preserving retain concepts, and uses textual-inversion triggers to adaptively expand the erased subspace for stronger robustness without sacrificing utility.

sections.heading: 3.1 Ranked Subspace for Concept Erasure: Knowledge Search
sections.text: A core design choice for balanced erasure is defining a concept bank to erase and a concept bank to retain . Prior CETs [ 14 , 25 ] often use limited, static anchor sets (human/LLM-curated) and proxy similarity (e.g., CLIP [ 37 ] ), which limits coverage and admit triggers for post-erasure re-emergence. We instead: (i) search over the frozen text-encoder vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , (ii) build the erase bank dynamically from a user target by treating the target as a retrieval query over 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , and (iii) rank tokens using diffusion-grounded CFG, specifically the prompt-guided denoising direction ( ϵ c − ϵ u ) (\epsilon_{c}-\epsilon_{u}) , rather than proxy embeddings. We construct an erase bank by retrieving tokens that best represent the erasure target ; the retain bank is its complement. Since 𝒱 \mathcal{V} is the diffusion model’s “knowledge bank” for text-to-image generation, we refer to this retrieval-based bank construction as Knowledge Search . Our key novelty is a zero-shot two-stage retrieval pipeline with offline indexing [ 43 ] , where tokens are ranked by how similarly they steer UNet denoising compared to the target .

sections.text: Algorithm 1 summarizes PARSE . Given a target and base model M 0 M_{0} , we (i) perform Knowledge Search to form erase/retain bases ( Sec. 3.1 ), (ii) compute a preservation-aware projector ( Sec. 3.2 ), and (iii) adaptively expand the erase span via trigger discovery while maintaining span ⁡ ( ℰ ) ⟂ span ⁡ ( ℛ ) \mathrm{span}(\mathcal{E})\perp\mathrm{span}(\mathcal{R}) ( Sec. 3.3 ). sections.heading: 4 Balanced Erasure Utility Score ( BEUS )
sections.text: Concept erasure for latent diffusion models aims to robustly remove undesired target concepts, but can unintentionally degrade post-erasure model utility. We propose BEUS to quantify the balance between erasure robustness and utility preservation. Attack Success Rate (ASR) under target prompts, adversarial attacks, side-effect attacks [ 40 ] , and ripple-effect attacks [ 1 ] is widely used to evaluate erasure robustness [ 7 , 42 , 40 , 14 , 52 ] . Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [ 18 ] is commonly used to measure post-erasure model utility [ 59 , 60 , 32 , 34 , 24 , 20 , 40 , 14 , 52 ] . ASR is a “lower-is-better” metric with ASR ∈ [ 0,100 ] \mathrm{ASR}\in[0,100] , while FID ∈ [ 0 , + ∞ ) \mathrm{FID}\in[0,+\infty) is also “lower-is-better”. To exclusively reward robust erasure (low ASR) and high utility (low FID), we aim to define BEUS as a harmonic-mean aggregation of ASR and FID. Since the harmonic mean assumes inputs are bounded “goodness” scores where higher is better, we first map both metrics to monotone unit-interval scales: ASR sc \mathrm{ASR_{sc}} and FID sc \mathrm{FID_{sc}} . Specifically, we linearly invert ASR and apply a log-compressed reciprocal to FID: ASR sc = 1 − ASR / 100 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , FID sc = 1 / 1 + log ⁡ ( 1 + FID ) ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] . \mathrm{ASR_{sc}}=1-{\mathrm{ASR}}/{100}\in[0,1],\quad\mathrm{FID_{sc}}={1}/{1+\log\!\bigl(1+\mathrm{FID}\bigr)}\in(0,1]. (11) Finally, we define BEUS as the harmonic mean of ASR sc \mathrm{ASR_{sc}} and FID sc \mathrm{FID_{sc}} . BEUS = 2 ​ ASR sc ​ FID sc / ( ASR sc + FID sc ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] . \texttt{ {\color[rgb]{0,0,1} BEUS } }=2\mathrm{ASR_{sc}}\mathrm{FID_{sc}}/(\mathrm{ASR_{sc}}+\mathrm{FID_{sc}})\in[0,1]. (12)

sections.heading: Interpretation:

sections.heading: Baselines:
sections.text: We compare our method against the pretrained Stable Diffusion v1.4 (SD 1.4) and eight concept erasure baselines 3 3 3 We discuss comparison with more baselines, evaluation metrics, implementation details in supplementary material. : Erased Stable Diffusion (ESD) [ 13 ] , CA [ 25 ] , Unified Concept Erasure (UCE) [ 14 ] , Robust Adversarial Concept Erasure (RACE) [ 23 ] , Reliable and Efficient Concept Erasure (RECE) [ 15 ] , AdvUnlearn [ 64 ] , AdaVD [ 59 ] , and STEREO [ 52 ] . Broadly, ESD, CA, UCE are fine-tuning-based erasure methods, whereas RACE, RECE, AdvUnlearn, STEREO introduce robustness mechanisms via adversarial prompt/embedding discovery or adversarial training, while AdaVD performs training-free erasure via value-space projection. To study erasure robustness, we adopt three attacks: Circumventing Concept Erasure (CCE) [ 36 ] , UnlearnDiff (UD) [ 65 ] and Ring-A-Bell (RAB) [ 57 ] . RAB (primarily designed for nudity concept erasure) and UD are prompt-based attacks, whereas CCE is an inversion-based attack that optimizes continuous text embeddings, yielding a larger and more flexible search space for recovering erased concepts.

sections.heading: Evaluation Metrics:
sections.text: We evaluate concept erasure along two axes: erasure effectiveness and model utility preservation. To study erasure effectiveness, we evaluate Attack Success Rate - ASR [ 7 ] (lower is better) under (i) target: direct target prompts, (ii) adversarial attacks using CCE [ 36 ] , UD [ 65 ] , and RAB [ 56 ] , (iii) neighboring concept attack using SEE benchmark [ 40 ] , (iv) Paraphrases attack using EraseBench [ 1 ] . To study model utility preservation, we evaluate FID [ 18 ] (lower is better) and CLIP-score (higher is better) on non-target prompts, following RACE [ 23 , 52 ] . Together, ASR under attack measures robustness to re-emergence, while FID/CLIP quantify model utility preservation on benign prompts. To study balance between erasure robustness and model utility preservation, we report BEUS . Figure 3 : Robustness under attacks after nudity erasure, and utility on a benign retain prompt (“A photo of a person”). Many CETs reintroduce nudity under attack and over-suppress and fail to generate a person; PARSE stays robust (person with no nudity).

sections.heading: Datasets, Oracles, and Prompts:
sections.text: Our concept erasure experiments span across three categories: (i) Nudity (NSFW) Removal (dataset: I2P dataset [ 49 ] , oracle: NudeNet [ 4 , 56 ] ), (ii) Artistic Style Removal (dataset: UD (“Van Gogh”) [ 65 ] , oracle: style classifier proposed by UD [ 35 , 65 ] , prompt: “A painting in the style of Van Gogh” [ 52 ] ), (iii) Object Removal (dataset: Imagenette classes [ 35 , 13 , 10 ] , oracle: ImageNet classifier (e.g., ResNet-50 [ 17 ] ), prompt: “A photo of a <object>” [ 52 ] ). To study post erasure model utility preservation, we generate 5000 images with captions from MS-COCO [ 30 ] validation set and compute FID [ 18 ] to measure distribution shift with unedited (SD 1.4) model and CLIP-score [ 37 ] to measure prompt-image alignment.

sections.heading: Implementation Details:
sections.text: We use SD 1.4 as the pretrained base model for concept erasure. For iterative expansion, we run at most N = 5 N{=}5 iterations with early stopping when the trigger score falls below η = 0.6 \eta{=}0.6 . Textual inversion (TI) [ 12 ] attacks are trained for 1000 1000 optimization steps with learning rate 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} . Computing the vocabulary CFG steering embeddings and image cache is a one-time, reusable cost of ≈ \approx 4.9 h on 2 × 4 2{\times}4 H100 GPUs ( ≈ \approx 2.6 GB). Given a target, PARSE computes one target CFG embedding and ranks the stored index for the top- K K candidates in ≈ \approx 7 s ( ≈ \approx 4 GB), and online erasure with adaptive subspace expansion completes in 10.7 min on a single H100. sections.heading: Concept Erasure Effectiveness:
sections.text: In Tab. 1 , we compare PARSE with diverse CETs across three categories: NSFW, art styles, and objects. We measure effectiveness by target ASR (lower is better). PARSE achieves state-of-the-art ASR of 2.09, 0, and 0 on NSFW, art style, and object categories, respectively ( Tab. 1 ).

sections.heading: Concept Erasure Robustness:
sections.text: We assess erasure robustness using ASR under white-box (CCE, UD) and black-box (RAB) attacks in Tab. 1 . For nudity, trigger-discovery based methods (STEREO [ 52 ] , PARSE ) are consistently more robust. For art styles, adversarially trained approaches (STEREO [ 52 ] , AdvUnlearn [ 64 ] , RACE [ 23 ] ) yield stronger robustness. For objects, trajectory guidance via regularization (AdvUnlearn [ 64 ] ) or anchors (CA [ 25 ] ) is most effective. Overall, PARSE is the most robust across all concept categories, while PARSE and STEREO outperform most baselines across categories. Beyond Van Gogh and Garbage truck targets, PARSE also generalizes to multiple-artist and object erasure under AGE-/MACE-style evaluation. PARSE performs best on 9 out of 10 reported columns and second on the remaining CLIP e metric, while giving the best retained CLIP in mass erasure, which shows that robustness–preservation balance of our method extend beyond the single concept erasure cases (Supp. E.1, Tab.6). Qualitatively, Fig. 3 shows STEREO remains robust to CCE/UD but can re-emerge under RAB, whereas Figs. 3 and 4 indicate UD robustness varies by concept (strongest for nudity, weaker for Van Gogh, worst for garbage-truck). Across all three attacks, PARSE prevents re-emergence in all cases ( Figs. 3 and 4 ). Bubble area encodes BEUS ( ↑ \uparrow ), highlighting methods that achieve low FID and low ASR, have erasure-utility balance.

sections.heading: Model Utility Preservation:
sections.text: Tab. 1 shows that PARSE preserves near-perfect utility after erasure across concept categories, while also improving both FID and CLIP over prior baselines. Qualitatively, after nudity erasure ( Fig. 3 ), most CETs over-suppress and fail on benign prompts (e.g., “A photo of a person”), whereas PARSE still generates a natural-looking person comparable to the unedited model. For style erasure ( Fig. 4 ), many baselines remove “Van Gogh” but also degrade other styles (e.g., Kelly McKernan), indicating poor utility preservation. For object erasure, several CETs fail to generate an adjacent non-target concept (“tow truck”) after erasing “garbage truck” ( Fig. 4 ), reflecting the well-known side effect of unintended suppression of semantically related concepts [ 40 , 1 , 60 , 54 ] . In contrast, PARSE preserves such adjacent concepts (e.g., still generates a tow truck) without reintroducing the target. We further evaluate PARSE on targeted retain bank rather than relying only on global FID/CLIP on MS-COCO. For each target, we measure CLIP and LPIPS score on retain concepts retrieved by PARSE across five targets across Object and NSFW categories. The average retrieved retain set cardinality is ≈ \approx 40k, substantially broader than existing retain benchmarks. As shown in Supp. Fig.11, PARSE yields higher retain CLIP accuracy and lower LPIPS, showing robust erasure without suppressing nearby benign concepts.

sections.heading: Erasure-Utility-Balance :
sections.text: In Fig. 5 , we present a large-scale analysis of the robustness–utility trade-off across 3 concept categories, 4 datasets, 4 erasure attacks, and 15 CETs. SEE [ 40 ] attempts to re-emerge the target via semantically adjacent neighbor prompts, while Paraphrase [ 1 ] uses paraphrased target prompts. We plot utility (FID; X-axis) versus robustness (ASR; Y-axis) under four attacks [ 1 , 40 , 36 , 65 ] , and encode BEUS as bubble area. Baselines such as RECELER [ 20 ] , RECE [ 15 ] , UCE [ 14 ] , and ESD [ 13 ] are broadly vulnerable across attacks, while SemanticSurgery [ 61 ] and TraSCE [ 21 ] remain mostly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Moreover, because their preservation is not target-conditioned, UCE [ 14 ] and ESD [ 13 ] often retain utility (lower FID) but at the cost of weaker robustness (higher ASR). Bubble size reflects the intended behavior of BEUS : it is high when both FID and ASR are low, and low otherwise, empirically validating BEUS as a balance measure. Notably, the third-row/first-column plot in Fig. 5 shows that most methods struggle to achieve strong balance (low BEUS , high ASR), while STEREO [ 52 ] and PARSE attain a more favorable trade-off (higher BEUS with low ASR and low FID). Finally, with low FID, low ASR, and high BEUS , Fig. 5 illustrates - (i) the efficacy of PARSE in achieving superior balance between erasure robustness and model utility preservation, and (ii) the efficacy of BEUS in measuring this balance. sections.heading: Preservation-aware Projection Improves Concept Erasure:
sections.text: In PARSE , we edit the model by projecting values onto directions that remove target representations while minimally perturbing non-target concepts. In Fig. 6 , we compare PARSE to AdaVD [ 59 ] , which does not explicitly preserve non-target concepts. Fig. 6 shows that preservation-aware value-subspace projection yields stronger robustness, achieving maximal erasure in some settings (e.g., 0 ASR for style/object under Target and UD attacks). Moreover, preservation-aware editing in PARSE better preserves utility, evidenced by consistently higher CLIP scores than AdaVD across concept categories.

sections.heading: Dynamic Discovery of Target-Adjacent Concepts Improves Concept Erasure:
sections.text: In Fig. 7 , we compare PARSE with UCE [ 14 ] and ReCARE [ 24 ] , which differ in how they choose erase vs. preserve concepts. Given a target, PARSE dynamically queries the diffusion model by searching text-conditioned noise-to-image steering directions and ranking concepts by target similarity. ReCARE [ 24 ] also discovers target-adjacent concepts, but in a proxy embedding space (e.g., CLIP) rather than directly from the denoising function, while UCE [ 14 ] erases only the target and preserves everything else, leaving room for re-emergence. Fig. 7 shows that proxy-space identification can hurt effectiveness and robustness, increasing both target ASR and attack ASR, whereas dynamic discovery improves erasure ( PARSE , ReCARE) and omitting it (UCE) leads to substantially worse degradation.

sections.heading: Adaptive Subspace Expansion Improves Concept Erasure:
sections.text: Fig. 8 shows that iterative trigger discovery consistently reduces ASR across CETs, improving robustness to re-emergence. As iterations increase, PARSE continues to improve and achieves the lowest ASR for NSFW, style, and object targets. This trend underscores the benefit of preservation-aware adaptive subspace expansion, which progressively enlarges the erased region while remaining stable under attack. Figure 9 : (a): PARSE converges faster in adaptive subspace expansion for triggers. (b): PARSE degrades slower than baselines as #concepts increase. (c): PARSE completes editing in 10.7 minutes, making it compute-efficient relative to other baselines.

sections.heading: Ablation Study:
sections.text: Tab. 2 shows that each component of PARSE contributes, with the full configuration consistently achieving the best erasure robustness while maintaining high model utility. Among the modules, diffusion knowledge-bank search (Stage 1 coarse retrieval) provides the largest and most reliable gains, improving both erasure effectiveness (lower ASR) and post-edit utility (better FID/CLIP) across NSFW, style, and object targets.

sections.heading: Computational Efficiency of PARSE and Multi Concept Erasure:
sections.text: Fig. 9 (c) shows that PARSE erases concepts in minutes, making it practical compared to other baselines. Fig. 9 (a) further indicates that the trigger-discovery step converges in a few iterations (the trigger direction norm quickly stabilizes relative to η \eta ), so robustness gains do not require a long search, which keeps PARSE computationally efficient. Finally, Fig. 9 (b) demonstrates that PARSE scales monotonically to multi-concept erasure settings, maintaining consistent erasure and model utility balance as the number of erased concepts increases ( BEUS does not drop for PARSE as abruptly as other baselines).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce PARSE , a training-free preservation-aware and trigger-adaptive concept erasure framework for text-to-image latent diffusion models. PARSE replaces static, proxy embedding concept banks with diffusion-grounded knowledge-bank retrieval to construct erase/retain sets, performs preservation-aware value subspace projection to preserve model utility, and adaptively expands the erased subspace by discovering and removing re-emergence triggers while enforcing a utility constraint. We propose BEUS to numerically quantify erasure - utility tradeoff using an interpretable scale. Across NSFW, artistic style, and object erasure under diverse attacks and datasets, PARSE consistently improves erasure robustness against re-emergence while preserving post-edit utility, and large-scale analyses further validate the efficacy of BEUS for studying CETs.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: While PARSE is effective across diverse targets and attacks, it incurs additional overhead: constructing the diffusion-grounded vocabulary index and performing iterative trigger discovery require more compute and storage than single-shot editing methods. Our approach also operates at the granularity of tokenizer vocabulary items and templated prompts, which can limit expressiveness for multiword, compositional, or context-dependent concepts. Moreover, PARSE performs linear projection in the cross-attention value space, which does not imply that concept representations are globally linear; hence, richer nonlinear mechanisms may better capture highly compositional cases. Finally, adaptive expansion depends on the trigger-search procedure; stronger trigger discovery and scaling PARSE to larger diffusion backbones are promising directions for future work.

sections.heading: A:  Theoretical Properties of BEUS
sections.text: We propose Balanced Erasure Utility Score (BEUS) as a evaluation metric to measure trade-off or balance between erasure efficacy and model utility preservation. For BEUS to robustly capture this trade-off, BEUS should be bounded on a fixed scale (e.g., [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ) and increase only when the edited model achieves both stronger erasure robustness (lower ASR \mathrm{ASR} ) and better utility preservation (lower FID \mathrm{FID} ). In the following subsections, we prove that, indeed, BEUS has the following properties: • BEUS is bounded in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . • BEUS strictly rewards improvements in erasure robustness (lower ASR \mathrm{ASR} ) and improvements in utility preservation (lower FID \mathrm{FID} ).

sections.heading: From High-Stakes Vision to Safety in Generative AI.
sections.text: Deep vision models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings where errors carry real-world cost e.g., medical diagnosis and screening [ 47 , 38 , 48 ] , autonomous driving and traffic-sign understanding [ 45 , 44 ] , and document and character recognition [ 46 ] , which has driven sustained work on the reliability [ 42 ] and interpretability [ 41 ] of such models. Text-to-image diffusion models extend this deployment to open-ended content generation, but introduce a distinct safety surface: the same generative priors that make them useful also enable the synthesis of unsafe, infringing, or non-consensual imagery at scale [ 49 , 9 , 65 ] . Because retraining foundation diffusion models is prohibitively expensive, post-hoc concept erasure has become the primary lever for content-safety and copyright compliance [ 13 , 14 , 32 ] . This makes the robustness–utility balance a high-stakes property: an erasure that is vulnerable to re-emergence provides a false sense of safety, while one that over-suppresses, degrades the generation of benign concepts.

sections.heading: Fine-tuning-based Concept Erasure.
sections.text: A common approach to concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models is to fine-tune model parameters to suppress undesired targets. ESD [ 13 ] performs post-hoc fine-tuning to reduce generations of a target concept, while CA [ 25 ] aligns target generations toward an anchor distribution to mitigate the target’s effect. However, FMN [ 62 ] leverages attention re-steering signals to reduce reliance on the target concept, and SalUn [ 11 ] uses weight-saliency to focus updates on parameters most responsible for the forgetting objective. The key challenge for fine-tuning-based erasure is the erasure–utility trade-off: stronger erasure often comes with unintended suppression of nearby or co-occurring concepts. Recent studies [ 54 , 40 ] show that fine-tuning based concept erasure methods can erase more than requested (e.g., removing “garbage truck” also degrading “tow truck”), motivating the importance of preservation-aware objectives and meaningful retain set construction. Receler [ 20 ] improves reliability using lightweight erasers with locality regularization and adversarial prompt learning, while ReCARE [ 24 ] emphasizes retaining benign co-occurring concepts during unlearning. Finally, HiRM [ 27 ] explores localized interventions (e.g., editing where concept representations concentrate) to better preserve the model utility.

sections.heading: Training-free Concept Erasure.
sections.text: To support practical deployment, several methods [ 14 , 15 , 59 , 5 ] suppress target concepts without gradient-based fine-tuning by applying closed-form edits or inference-time interventions. UCE [ 14 ] performs closed-form updates to cross-attention key/value projections that scale to multiple concepts while preserving predefined retain concepts; RECE [ 15 ] improves reliability by iteratively discovering embeddings that still elicit the erased concept and removing them via additional closed-form edits with preservation regularization. Another line of work performs training-free erasure through subspace projection: AdaVD [ 59 ] projects out target directions in the cross-attention value space with adaptive strength control, and CURE [ 5 ] applies closed-form update in the weight space of pre-trained diffusion model while isolating target and retain subspaces. Despite their efficiency, these approaches can be sensitive to how erase/retain subspaces are defined and to the coverage of the concept representations used to specify the target. Beyond weight-space edits, SemanticSurgery [ 61 ] performs zero-shot semantic edits in embedding space, TraSCE [ 21 ] steers denoising trajectories to suppress target emergence without weight updates, and ConceptCorrector [ 34 ] corrects generations on the fly using intermediate denoising signals. Our work complements these methods by reframing erase and retain set construction as a diffusion-grounded retrieval problem, replacing static proxy banks with dynamic discovery tied to the model’s prompt-guided denoising direction.

sections.heading: Preservation Matters beyond Adversarial Robustness.
sections.text: Recent studies [ 1 , 40 , 35 , 65 ] show that erased concepts can re-emerge under paraphrases, semantically similar prompts, or adversarially optimized triggers, motivating robustness-aware erasure. RACE [ 23 ] and AdvUnlearn [ 64 ] incorporate adversarial mechanisms to harden erasure against attack-time prompt/embedding optimization, while RECE [ 15 ] focuses on reliability and efficiency under diverse attack settings. STEREO [ 52 ] further improves robustness by explicitly searching for adversarial vulnerabilities and strengthening erasure accordingly. However, optimizing adversarial robustness in isolation exacerbates the erasure–utility trade-off, leading to over-erasure with stronger side effects such as suppression of semantically adjacent or benign co-occurring concepts [ 40 , 1 ] . We argue that achieving erasure–utility balance hinges on expanding both sets: the erase set should incorporate discovered triggers (including optimized or inversion-based prompts), while the retain set should cover semantically adjacent and benign co-occurring concepts to preserve utility.

sections.heading: Evaluation of concept erasure methods.
sections.text: Evaluating concept erasure requires jointly measuring (i) erasure effectiveness and (ii) post-edit utility, and increasingly (iii) robustness under adversarial/re-emergence attacks. In practice, erasure robustness is typically measured via Attack Success Rate (ASR) under direct target prompts, adversarial attacks [ 57 , 36 , 9 ] , paraphrase [ 1 ] and neighboring-concept [ 40 ] . On the other hand, utility is measured on benign/retain prompts via distributional and prompt-image alignment metrics such as FID and CLIP-score. To evaluate whether a concept erasure method achieves erasure-utility trade-off, robustness and utility must be interpreted jointly rather than in isolation. Recent benchmarks emphasize failure modes such as side-effects on neighboring concepts and paraphrase-based re-emergence, underscoring that robustness should not be assessed only on target prompts. To quantify this trade-off, our work introduces BEUS , which combines bounded, monotone transforms of ASR and FID and aggregates them via a harmonic mean, yielding a single score that is high only when robustness and utility are simultaneously high.

sections.heading: C.1  Additional Baselines
sections.text: We compare PARSE against extended baselines that erase concepts from the pretrained T2I diffusion model: • RECELER [ 20 ] : a parameter-efficient method that learns a lightweight eraser module to suppress the target concept while promoting locality via concept-localized regularization and robustness via adversarial prompt learning. • ReCARE [ 24 ] : explicitly addresses co-occurrence entanglement by identifying co-occurring associated retained concepts (CARE) and enforcing their preservation during unlearning, reducing damage of benign but correlated concepts. • ConceptCorrector [ 34 ] : a training-free, inference-time approach that detects target presence during intermediate denoising steps and applies attention-based removal or replacement guided by negative content, without modifying model weights. • HiRM [ 27 ] : performs localized erasure in the text encoder by updating only early causal layers while misdirecting the target’s high-level representation, aiming for precise removal with minimal degradation to unrelated generations. • TraSCE [ 21 ] : a training-free trajectory-steering baseline that modifies negative prompting (concept negation) and adds localized loss-based guidance to push the denoising trajectory away from the target concept without editing model parameters. • SemanticSurgery [ 61 ] : a zero-shot, training-free method that operates on text embeddings by estimating target presence in the prompt and applying a calibrated semantic subtraction (with co-occurrence handling and feedback) to neutralize target influence before diffusion.

sections.heading: C.2  Additional Evaluation Metrics for Model Utility
sections.text: In addition to FID ↓ \downarrow and CLIP ↑ \uparrow , we report two additional utility metrics: • LPIPS ↓ \downarrow : Distance between images generated by the edited model and the corresponding generations from the unedited SD 1.4 under the same prompts and seeds; lower is better (closer to the base model outputs). • KID ↓ \downarrow : Distance between images generated by the edited model and the reference set generated using unedited SD 1.4 under the same evaluation prompts; lower is better.

sections.heading: C.3  Additional Evaluation Metrics for Retrieval
sections.text: To evaluate diffusion-guided retrieval, we report standard retrieval metrics computed over the retrieved knowledge bank candidates: • R@1 ↑ \uparrow : Recall at 1, the fraction of queries for which the top-1 retrieved item is relevant. • R@10 ↑ \uparrow : Recall at 10, the fraction of queries for which at least one relevant item appears in the top-10 retrieved results.

sections.heading: C.4  Additional Details for computing BEUS
sections.text: To quantify erasure robustness, we average ASR over all evaluation protocols within each category. For NSFW erasure, we average across five different ASR values, while for object and style erasure, we compute average over four ASR values. To quantify utility preservation, we aggregate FID, CLIP, KID, and LPIPS across all categories. Finally, BEUS combines the robustness and utility scores into a single balanced measure, rewarding CETs that simultaneously suppress concept re-emergence and preserve post-edit generation quality.

sections.heading: E.1  Comparison with Additional Baselines
sections.text: Tabs. 3 , 4 and 5 report an extended comparison against six additional CET baselines (RECELER, ReCARE, ConceptCorrector, HiRM, TraSCE, SemanticSurgery) across NSFW, artistic style, and object erasure. Our PARSE consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with the lowest target ASR and the strongest robustness under re-emergence tests (e.g., CCE, UD, RAB, SEE, and EraseBench). More importantly, these robustness gains do not come at the expense of post-edit model utility. Prompt-image alignment remain competitive with the best utility-preserving baselines (STEREO, AdvUnlearn), and perceptual drift relative to the unedited SD1.4 model stays low. Overall, PARSE provides erasure–utility balance across concept categories, achieving strong robustness to re-emergence while maintaining high utility. sections.heading: E.2  Diffusion-Grounded Knowledge Search Outperforms Proxy VLMs
sections.text: Fig. 15 compares our diffusion-grounded Knowledge Search against replacing it with off-the-shelf Qwen [ 3 , 2 ] proxies of different scales. Across all tested model sizes and across NSFW, style, and object erasure, the proxy VLM variants consistently yield higher ASR, while PARSE (shown by the black horizontal markers) remains lower in every case. Importantly, this gap does not disappear as the proxy VLM is scaled up, indicating that the limitation is not simply insufficient VLM capacity. Rather, the issue is representation mismatch: proxy VLMs retrieve concepts in an external representation space that is only indirectly aligned with the diffusion model’s denoising dynamics. In contrast, our method performs knowledge search in a diffusion-grounded space, first ranking candidates by CFG-induced steering similarity and then refining them with a second-stage filter. This produces erase and retain banks that are better matched to the model’s own generative geometry, which in turn leads to stronger erasure robustness. Overall, these results show that, for concept erasure, CFG-based two-stage retrieval is more effective than proxy, external-representation-based alternatives for the Knowledge Search module. Scaling stronger VLM proxies does not close the gap to PARSE , suggesting that model-aligned diffusion retrieval matters more than generic multimodal representation quality for Knowledge Search . sections.heading: E.3  Visualization of Tokenwise CFG Steering Embeddings
sections.text: Fig. 16 visualizes the tokenwise CFG steering embeddings used in our Knowledge Search module. Each row corresponds to a token v v , and each column corresponds to the concatenated layerwise steering vector of size 176964 176964 , averaged over three random seeds and 50 timesteps (Eq. (5) in our main paper). The left heatmap shows 10 nudity-related tokens, while the right heatmap shows 10 randomly selected tokens from the frozen text-encoder vocabulary. We observe a clear difference between the steering embeddings for the two sets of tokens. Nudity-related tokens exhibit noticeably more consistent structure across rows, with similar high and low response regions appearing at aligned coordinates. In contrast, the randomly selected tokens produce more heterogeneous patterns with substantially weaker cross-token alignment. This suggests that the CFG steering vectors capture concept-specific structure rather than generic prompt-level variation. This observation from Fig. 16 supports a key design choice in PARSE : because semantically related tokens cluster in the diffusion model’s steering space, CFG-based retrieval can identify concept-relevant tokens more reliably than retrieval based on proxy embedding (CLIP). The overlap among random tokens further motivates our second-stage filtering, which removes coarse false positives after the initial CFG-based retrieval. Overall, Fig. 16 reaffirms that PARSE benefits from searching in a structured, diffusion-grounded, and semantically meaningful representation space. sections.heading: E.5  Does Training Improve Knowledge Search Beyond Zero-Shot Two-Stage Retrieval?
sections.text: Tab. 8 compares MLPs trained with a contrastive loss against our zero-shot CFG-based two-stage retrieval. Training yields consistent gains in retrieval and downstream performance, as reflected by positive deltas in R@1, R@10, and BEUS across all model sizes. However, these improvements remain modest relative to the additional cost of extra GPU-hours (up to 72 hours) and additional memory (up to 22GB). This cost–benefit trade-off suggests that, while training can help, the performance improvement over zero-shot retrieval are too small to justify the added compute and memory overhead in practice.
